name: Nikhil Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello Nikhil, thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential and your name won't be attached to it. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run an electric rope shovel at an iron ore mine, the big one with a bucket you could park two cars in. I'm lead operator on my rotation, so I set the dig plan with the geologist at the start of shift and talk the truck drivers into position. Two weeks on, one week off, I fly in and out. Loading a truck in three passes, clean, no spill, that still feels good after six years.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What else fills the day, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: On my breaks I'm usually on my phone with an AI tutor, I'm halfway through an automation technician certificate online. The camp food wears me out, honestly, and the flights. My partner Lena's a graphic designer, she works from home in the city, and two weeks away is long. On my week off I cook for three days straight just to remember what vegetables taste like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. Mostly hype. That would be a surprise to me, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was overcooked. At work I'd probably get teased, because I'm the guy always showing people what the AI can do. I'd laugh along.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be a bit let down. I've bet some of my spare time on this, the certificate, the nights learning. But a quiet decade isn't bad for a shovel operator, so I'd just carry on and still finish the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep my roster, finish the automation certificate by mid next year because it's still useful for the remote systems we've already got. Keep saving, I've got about five months of bills now. Maybe me and Lena finally take the trip to her grandparents' village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Slightly bored, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Bored how?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like when things move. When the mine put in the new fleet tracking system, I was the one who read the manual on the plane. If the big change never comes, I'm still digging the same benches at forty, which is fine, but it's a long time to be fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lena see it the same way?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she'd be relieved. Her work is the stuff the image tools can already half do, logos and layouts. So in this picture she sleeps better, and I'd take that trade any day. Her sleeping better is worth more than me being less bored.

S0.say: Fair enough, the hype was overcooked. I'm the guy always showing people what the AI can do, so I'd get teased at work and laugh along.
S0.think: I'd be a bit let down, because I've bet my spare time on this. But a quiet decade isn't bad for a shovel operator, so I'd carry on and still finish the course.
S0.do: Keeps his fly-in fly-out roster and finishes the automation technician certificate by mid next year. Keeps saving, at about five months of bills, and plans a trip with Lena to her grandparents' village.
S0.feel: Calm and slightly bored, but glad his partner would sleep better.
S0.quote: If the big change never comes, I'm still digging the same benches at forty, which is fine, but it's a long time to be fine.
S0.fieldNote: Nikhil is the rare operator who is mildly disappointed by a calm future. He uses AI daily to study and enjoys change for its own sake. His partner's job as a designer is more exposed than his, and he puts her peace of mind above his own boredom.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. This is the one I'd bet on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a chance to make mining safer and fairer if we don't let the company keep all the savings. At work I'd tell the crew to get trained early. Online I'd post about a robot tax, I'd probably get into a few arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, I think it's good. Shovels go remote, I'm already trained for the remote room, I move up. But I'd feel guilty about it, because for every one of me there's three guys who don't want to learn and won't be asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd put my name down for the remote operations centre in the city, which would also mean living with Lena full time. I'd finish the certificate faster, by Easter. I'd help run lunch sessions on the remote system for the crew, and I'd push the union to demand paid training for everyone, not just volunteers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and a bit excited, with guilt sitting next to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned moving to the city. What does that change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everything, good stuff. No more flights, no more camp food, I'm home every night. Lena's work might be getting squeezed in this picture, so me being steady and home would matter more. We'd probably stop renting the tiny flat and look for something a bit bigger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said guilt. Who are you thinking of?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Big Tony, who runs the second shovel. Forty-eight, brilliant, can feel a boulder through the controls before the camera sees it. He told me once he's never sending an email in his life. I'd want the company to give him real time to learn, paid, not a two-hour session and a quiz.

S1.say: This is a chance to make mining safer and fairer if the company doesn't keep all the savings. I'd tell the crew to train early and post online about a robot tax.
S1.think: For me it's good: shovels go remote, I'm already trained, I move up. But I'd feel guilty, because for every one of me there are three guys who won't be asked or won't want to learn.
S1.do: Applies to the remote operations centre in the city in the first month and finishes his certificate by Easter. Runs lunch sessions on the remote system for his crew and pushes the union for paid training for everyone.
S1.feel: Calm and a bit excited, with guilt alongside.
S1.quote: For every one of me there's three guys who don't want to learn and won't be asked.
S1.fieldNote: Nikhil sees this scenario as a promotion and a way home to his partner. His progressive views show up as guilt and as a push for paid training for colleagues like Big Tony. He's the first person to volunteer, which fits his early-adopter habits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay. That's different. That's the whole thing at once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the gains shared out, properly, starting now: a robot tax and a public income. At work I'd say don't panic, but don't sit still either. Online I'd be posting a lot, probably too much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my clever plan doesn't work here. The remote room is the next thing to go, because if an AI can do any job, it can watch a screen. I'd be first in, then first out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still take the remote job if offered, because it's more money and I'm home. I'd put every spare dollar into savings, aim for a year. I'd start building something on the side with the AI tools, maybe helping small mining contractors set up their own systems, while there's still a window for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not frozen, but the floor's moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does two years of warning get you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much, but more than most people have. I know the tools, so I can be useful for a year or so while everyone else is catching up. That's a short boat ride, but it's a boat. After that, I'm in the same place as everyone else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Lena say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd say we're both in trouble now, not just her. And we'd talk about whether we still try for kids in a few years, which we'd planned. I think we'd wait. I hate that, but I think we would.

S2.say: We need the gains shared out properly, starting now, with a robot tax and a public income. Don't panic, but don't sit still either.
S2.think: My clever plan doesn't work here, because if an AI can do any job, it can watch a screen. I'd be first into the remote room and then first out.
S2.do: Takes the remote job if offered and aims to save a year of bills. Starts a side business helping small mining contractors set up AI systems while there's still a window, and puts off plans to have children.
S2.feel: Anxious, not frozen, but feeling the floor move.
S2.quote: I'd be first in, then first out.
S2.fieldNote: Even the most adaptable person in the crew sees his edge shrink to about a year here. Nikhil still acts fast, taking the remote job and starting a side business. The decision to delay children was quiet and clearly painful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. Okay, that's a different game.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is long enough to get the policy right if we start in year one. I'd go to union meetings and to my local member's office with some proper numbers. At work, I'd keep the lunch sessions going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, five years is good for me. I get three or four strong years in the remote room, I save, I learn everything about how these systems are set up. By the time they don't need me, I've got money and a skill nobody else in my town has.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Take the remote centre job in the first few months. Put a third of my pay into savings and a small share portfolio, mostly the companies building the robots, which feels a bit like betting against myself. Keep teaching the crew. Maybe help start a workers' co-op that bids for the rehab contracts when the pit closes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly busy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said betting against yourself. Can you say more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the robots win, the companies that make them win, so owning a tiny bit is a hedge. It feels wrong for someone who votes the way I do. But Lena's dad put his savings in the mine company's shares for years, and that's what paid off their house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the difference between this and the two-year one, for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm reacting. Five years, I'm planning. With five I can set something up with people I trust, the co-op idea, instead of just grabbing what I can on my own.

S3.say: Five years is long enough to get the policy right if we start in year one. I'd bring proper numbers to union meetings and my local member's office.
S3.think: Five years is good for me: three or four strong years in the remote room, saving and learning how the systems are set up. By the time they don't need me, I've got money and a rare skill.
S3.do: Takes the remote centre job within months and puts a third of his pay into savings and a small share portfolio in robot makers. Keeps teaching his crew and explores a workers' co-op to bid for rehabilitation contracts.
S3.quote: I can set something up with people I trust, the co-op idea, instead of just grabbing what I can on my own.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Nikhil moves from reacting to planning, and his ideas turn collective, like a co-op. He openly admits that investing in robot makers clashes with his politics, and justifies it with his father-in-law's example. He's the only person so far who sees himself benefiting for several years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be thirty-seven. I'd be ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the best-case version of AGI, so let's not waste it. We could build a proper public safety net and training system in ten years. I'd be loud about it, online and at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd do well for most of the ten years. I'd be the one setting up the systems that replace my old crew, which I'd have mixed feelings about. At the end I'd be out like everyone, but older, with savings and maybe a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Year one, I'd keep the shovel job and finish the certificate, then move to the remote centre. I'd join a group at the union pushing for retraining money. Lena and I would buy a small place and try for a kid, because ten years feels like enough room to do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy and hopeful at the same time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd set up the systems that replace your old crew. How would you live with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By making sure it's not done behind their backs. If I'm in the room, I can tell them six months early, not two weeks. I can push for their redeployment. Someone's going to do it, better it's someone who knows Tony's name.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the hardest part of the ten-year picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Knowing the end point is the same, and still choosing to have a kid. That's a bet on there being a decent world after work. I think we'd make it anyway, but I'd want to know someone serious was building that world.

S4.say: This is the best-case version of AGI, so let's not waste it. We could build a proper public safety net and training system in ten years.
S4.think: I'd do well for most of the ten years, setting up the systems that replace my old crew, which I'd feel mixed about. At the end I'd be out like everyone, but older, with savings and maybe a house.
S4.do: Keeps the shovel job and finishes the certificate in year one, then moves to the remote centre. Joins a union group pushing for retraining money, and buys a small place with Lena and tries for a child.
S4.feel: Uneasy and hopeful at the same time.
S4.quote: Someone's going to do it, better it's someone who knows Tony's name.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years lets Nikhil go ahead with family plans he'd delay under faster timelines. He accepts that he'd help automate his old crew's jobs, and frames his role as giving them early warning. His hope rests on someone building a decent world after work, which he can't be sure of.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two years. In that one, the thing I'm good at, learning fast, buys me a year at most. What would help is a public income that's already designed before it's needed, and a robot tax so the money's there. And honestly, help for people like Big Tony, who'd need more time than me.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are scared of, versus what they say they're scared of. Most of the guys say they're scared of robots. What they're actually scared of is being useless at home. That's worth knowing.

headlineQuote: What they're actually scared of is being useless at home.
portrait: Nikhil Tanaka is 27 and the lead shovel operator on his rotation at a large iron ore mine, flying in and out from the city where his partner Lena works as a designer. He uses AI every day, mostly to study for an automation technician certificate, and he's the crew's early adopter. He has about five months of bills saved and leans left, so he feels guilty about doing well while older colleagues struggle. In slower scenarios he sees a promotion and a way home; in the two-year one his edge shrinks to about a year and he delays having children. With ten years he plans a house and a child, betting that someone will build a decent world after work.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because his skill at learning fast would only buy him about a year.
whatWouldHelp: A public income designed before it's needed, a robot tax to fund it, and extra help for older workers like Big Tony who'd need more time.
